content: Sensorineural hearing loss is a type of hearing impairment where the underlying cause is located in the vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII), the inner ear, or the central auditory processing centers of the brain. In individuals with this condition, the Weber test, which involves placing a vibrating tuning fork on the head, will localize sound to the unaffected ear. The Rinne test, which compares air conduction to bone conduction, remains positive (normal), although both air and bone conduction are equally diminished. Sensorineural hearing loss can be either congenital or acquired. Congenital Causes: Cochlear aplasia: This refers to the lack of development of the cochlea. Chromosomal syndromes: Rare genetic conditions can lead to sensorineural hearing loss. Congenital cholesteatoma: This involves the presence of squamous epithelium in abnormal locations, such as within the external auditory canal or the middle ear. In the middle ear, the simple epithelium transitions into ciliated pseudostratified epithelium lining the Eustachian tube (pharyngotympanic tube), which becomes continuous with the respiratory epithelium of the pharynx. Acquired Causes: Ototoxicity: Certain medications, such as aspirin, can damage the auditory system. Physical trauma: This may result from temporal bone fractures affecting the cochlea and middle ear or shearing injuries involving cranial nerve VIII. Noise-induced hearing loss: Prolonged exposure to loud noises exceeding 90 dB can lead to hearing loss, typically starting at 4000 Hz (high frequency). Normal human hearing ranges from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Presbyacusis: Age-related hearing loss, which predominantly affects high frequencies (4000 Hz to 8000 Hz). Vascular ischemia: Reduced blood flow to the inner ear or cranial nerve VIII can result in hearing loss. Perilymph fistula: This condition involves a rupture of the round or oval windows, leading to leakage of perilymph. Patients often experience vertigo or imbalance, and there is usually a history of trauma or events that increased intracranial pressure. Autoimmune inner ear disease: Prompt administration of steroids directly into the ear is necessary to manage this condition. Cerebellopontine angle tumors: These tumors, located at the junction of the pons and cerebellum, can compress cranial nerves VII and VIII, leading to symptoms such as hearing loss, facial weakness, or imbalance. Examples include: Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma): A benign tumor arising from Schwann cells. Meningioma: A benign tumor originating from the pia and arachnoid mater. Ménière's disease: This condition causes sensorineural hearing loss in the low-frequency range (125 Hz to 1000 Hz). It is characterized by sudden episodes of vertigo lasting minutes to hours, often preceded by tinnitus, a sensation of aural fullness, and fluctuating hearing loss. Treatment: Currently, sensorineural hearing loss is managed using hearing aids or cochlear implants. Hearing aids amplify sounds at specific frequencies to compensate for the hearing loss in those ranges. Cochlear implants, on the other hand, directly stimulate the cochlear nerve to restore auditory perception.
